8.text: A man who has an extra boat often gives the use of it to some of his

9.text: neighbors. It is contrary to the sense of justice of the natives to allow a

10.text: good boat to lie idle on shore, when near by are hunters in need of one.

11.text: In such a case a boat-crew is also formed, under the direction of one who is

12.text: considered to be the boat-master, and responsible for the boat. Nothing is

13.text: paid for the use of the boat, even when the hunt has been exceedingly suc-

14.text: cessful; as, for instance, when a whale has been killed. To pay for such use

15.text: is believed to endanger the “hunting-luck.” In the case of a very successful

16.text: hunt, however, the boat-master will immediately buy the boat, and thus have

18.text: To cite an example, Kuvaˊr told me that one year he was making a

19.text: trip to St. Lawrence Island in a boat that belonged to one of his neighbors.

20.text: On the way they had the very rare chance to kill a polar bear in the water.

21.text: Polar bears in the Pacific are much rarer than whales, though they bring less.

22.text: On returning home, Kuvaˊr kept the boat in his possession, and gave its

23.text: owner another boat of his own, which was much larger and of better con-

24.text: struction than the other. Kuvaˊr, it is true, is an Eskimo, but the same rule

25.text: exists among the Chukchee. On the other hand, when a man has killed a

26.text: whale for the first time in his life, he must sell his boat and buy another.

27.text: When I asked for the reason of this custom, the natives explained that it was a

28.text: kind of sacrifice to the killed whale. The owner gives away the boat that

29.text: has helped to kill the whale, and takes another, “still innocent.”

30.text: The boat-master sits at the helm. This is the place of honor, and his

31.text: by right. Among the Russians and the Russianized natives of the Kolyma,

32.text: Indighirka, and other polar rivers, the place of the master is always with the

33.text: hand on the helm. Even when a local trader travels on the river with hired

34.text: assistants, he sits at the helm. He who leaves this place to another man,

35.text: and sits idly in the middle of the boat, is considered effeminate.

36.text: The Chukchee families are so small, that the eight or six members of

37.text: the crew may belong to four or even five families. Moreover, a father and

38.text: son often count as but one paddler, because they replace each other. The

39.text: elderly father goes only on the shorter trips; the son, on the long autumn

40.text: expeditions, when the sea is rough and the cold severe. Among the families

41.text: that form the boat’s crew, besides the relatives, may also be included the

42.text: families of friends, of close neighbors. All such families have their houses in
